lessons.title: Line and Shape
lessons.thesis: Before light and color there is the skeleton: where the edges are and what shapes they enclose.
lessons.intro: Every picture, however realistic, can be reduced to a handful of lines and flat shapes. In this lesson the café scene is stripped down to that skeleton. Notice how much of the picture's character is already decided before any shading or color arrives.
lessons.exercise: Squint at the control image until the details vanish. Count the big shapes you can still see. If the answer is more than seven, the picture is probably cluttered.

cards.name: Contour Outline
cards.subtitle: A line around every form
cards.explanation: A contour is the line that traces the outer edge of a thing. Nature has no outlines, so drawing one is the first act of interpretation: it declares where one object ends and the next begins.
look: A single even line encloses the figure, chair and cup
Inner lines mark only the big folds and overlaps
With no shading at all, the scene is still fully readable

cards.name: Line Weight
cards.subtitle: Thick and thin
cards.explanation: A line that swells and thins feels alive. Thicker lines pull forward and suggest weight or shadow, while thin lines recede and suggest light or distance.
look: Lines thicken on the underside of forms, where shadow would fall
The nearest objects carry the heaviest lines
Thin lines on the window side make that edge feel lit

cards.name: Line Direction
cards.subtitle: Horizontal, vertical, diagonal, curved
cards.explanation: The dominant direction of a picture's lines sets its mood before the subject does. Horizontals rest, verticals stand firm, diagonals move and curves flow.
look: Horizontals make the café feel calm and settled
Diagonals make the same room feel restless
Curves soften everything, including the figure

cards.name: Implied Line
cards.subtitle: Lines that are not drawn
cards.explanation: The eye connects things without being asked. A gaze, a pointing hand or a row of objects creates a line that exists only in the viewer's head, and it steers attention as strongly as a drawn one.
look: Her gaze makes a line from her eyes to its target
The viewer's eye follows that line and lands where she looks
A row of objects on the table forms a second invisible line

cards.name: Hard, Soft and Lost Edges
cards.subtitle: How one shape meets the next
cards.explanation: An edge can be razor-sharp, blurred or missing entirely where two similar tones merge. Sharp edges attract the eye, and lost edges let the viewer's imagination finish the form.
look: The sharpest edge in the picture is at the face
Hair and shoulder melt into the dark background on the shadow side
You still read the whole figure, even where no edge exists

cards.name: Silhouette
cards.subtitle: The shape with the inside removed
cards.explanation: Fill a figure with solid black and you learn whether its shape alone tells the story. A clear silhouette reads instantly, and a confusing one stays confusing however well it is rendered.
look: The crossed legs, cup and profile are all identifiable from outline alone
Gaps between arm and body keep the shape readable
Where limbs overlap the torso, information is lost

cards.name: Shape Language
cards.subtitle: Circles, squares and triangles
cards.explanation: Simple shapes carry feeling. Round shapes feel friendly and soft, square shapes feel stable and solid, and triangular shapes feel sharp, fast or dangerous.
look: In the round version, hair, cup, chair and table all echo circles
The square version feels sturdier and more formal
The triangular version looks edgy, though the pose has not changed

images.label: Variant 3 — Triangles. Keep pose and layout

cards.name: Positive and Negative Space
cards.subtitle: The thing and the gap around it
cards.explanation: The figure is positive space, and the empty areas around and between forms are negative space. Good designers shape the gaps as carefully as the objects.
look: The gap between arm and body is a shape in its own right
The space between chair legs repeats and varies
When the colors flip, the background becomes the subject

images.label: Variant 1 — Figure and furniture in flat black on white
Variant 2 — The same image inverted: white figure, black surroundings

cards.name: Big, Medium, Small
cards.subtitle: Variety of shape size
cards.explanation: Pictures with shapes of all one size feel monotonous. A common design habit is one big shape, a few medium ones and a scatter of small accents.
look: One large mass dominates: the figure with her chair
The table and window are the medium shapes
The cup, glasses and small details are the accents

lessons.title: Value
lessons.thesis: Value is how light or dark something is. It does most of the work in a picture, and color takes the credit.
lessons.intro: Remove all color from a good picture and it still works. Remove the pattern of lights and darks and it collapses. This lesson shows the café in gray so you can see that pattern alone, then pushes it lighter, darker, simpler and stronger.
lessons.exercise: Turn your phone screen to grayscale and look at any three cards from later lessons. Which one loses the most? That picture was leaning on color instead of value.

cards.name: Grayscale
cards.subtitle: The picture without its color
cards.explanation: Every color has a value, a position between white and black. Converting to gray reveals the structure underneath: which areas are light, which are dark, and whether the subject separates from its surroundings.
look: The figure still stands out from the background
Some colors that looked different turn out to be the same gray
The window is the lightest shape and the eye goes there first

cards.name: Two-Value Design
cards.subtitle: Notan: only black and white
cards.explanation: Notan is a Japanese term for the design of light against dark. Forcing every tone to pure black or pure white shows whether the picture has a strong underlying pattern.
look: Everything in light becomes white and everything in shadow becomes black
Shadow shapes merge into a few large black masses
The scene is recognizable from two flat tones

cards.name: Three-Value Plan
cards.subtitle: Light, middle, dark
cards.explanation: Most painters plan with three values before anything else. One of the three usually covers most of the picture, which gives the image a clear overall tone.
look: Middle gray covers the largest area
White is saved for the window and the lit side of the figure
Black appears only in a few accents

cards.name: High Key
cards.subtitle: Mostly light values
cards.explanation: A high-key picture lives in the top of the value scale, with pale tones and few true darks. It feels airy, gentle, clean or dreamy.
look: The darkest dark is only a middle gray
Shadows are soft and pale
The mood is light and open

cards.name: Low Key
cards.subtitle: Mostly dark values
cards.explanation: A low-key picture lives in the bottom of the scale, with deep tones and a few small lights. It feels intimate, serious, mysterious or dramatic.
look: Most of the frame is dark
A small area of light on the face and cup carries the picture
The room's edges disappear into shadow

cards.name: Value Contrast
cards.subtitle: Wide range or narrow range
cards.explanation: The distance between a picture's lightest light and darkest dark sets its energy. A wide range is punchy and dramatic, and a narrow range is quiet and misty.
look: The full-range version uses both pure white and pure black
The narrow version uses only middle grays
The same scene feels loud in one and hushed in the other

images.label: Variant 1 — Full range from black to white
Variant 2 — Compressed to middle grays only

cards.name: Value Grouping
cards.subtitle: The squint test
cards.explanation: Strong pictures keep their lights together and their darks together instead of scattering them like confetti. Squinting blurs the detail and shows whether the big groups hold.
look: Small lights inside the shadow stay darker than anything in the light
Blurred, the picture reads as a few large patches
The patches make a simple, memorable pattern

images.label: Variant 1 — The control with its lights and darks massed into large conne…
Variant 2 — The same image heavily blurred

cards.name: Counterchange
cards.subtitle: Light against dark, dark against light
cards.explanation: An edge is clearest when a light shape meets a dark one. Counterchange places each part of the subject against its opposite value, so the figure stays readable from head to foot.
look: Her lit side sits against a dark part of the background
Her shadow side sits against a light part
No edge of the figure is lost by accident

lessons.title: Light on Form
lessons.thesis: Light falling on a solid object always makes the same few zones. Learn their names and you can read any shaded picture.
lessons.intro: A ball, a cheek and a coffee cup all catch light the same way: a bright side, a dark side, and a predictable set of bands between and around them. This lesson isolates each zone on our model so you can find it in every later card.
lessons.exercise: Put a white mug beside a window. Find its highlight, its darkest band and its shadow on the table. Then slide a sheet of colored paper next to its dark side and watch the shadow change color.

cards.name: Light Side and Shadow Side
cards.subtitle: The two families
cards.explanation: Every lit form divides into a part that faces the light and a part that turns away. The first rule of shading is to keep the two families separate: nothing in shadow is as bright as anything in light.
look: A clear boundary runs down the face, arm and cup
Details inside the shadow stay quiet and dark
The form looks solid because the two sides never mix

cards.name: Highlight
cards.subtitle: The light source, mirrored
cards.explanation: A highlight is a small reflection of the light source itself. It sits where the surface angles the light straight into your eye, so it moves when you move and is sharpest on shiny things.
look: A crisp bright spot on the cup rim and glasses
A softer, broader one on the hair and cheek
Matte cloth has almost none

cards.name: Halftone and Terminator
cards.subtitle: Where the form turns away
cards.explanation: Between the highlight and the shadow, the surface darkens gradually as it turns from the light. These are the halftones. They end at the terminator, the line where direct light stops.
look: The cheek darkens smoothly toward the far side
A soft line marks where light gives way to shadow
That line follows the form's shape like a contour map

cards.name: Core Shadow
cards.subtitle: The darkest band on the form
cards.explanation: Just past the terminator lies a band darker than the rest of the shadow. Direct light cannot reach it, and bounced light from the room barely does. It is what makes round things look round.
look: A dark stripe runs down the shadow side of the cup
The same band appears on the arm and the cheek
The shadow beyond it is slightly lighter

cards.name: Bounce Light
cards.subtitle: Light reflected into the shadow
cards.explanation: Light hits the table, the wall and her clothes, then bounces back into the shadows, carrying the color of whatever it bounced from. It is why shadows are rarely black and never flat.
look: The underside of the chin glows faintly with the table's color
The shadow side of the cup picks up a tint from the saucer
The bounce is always dimmer than the lit side

cards.name: Cast Shadow
cards.subtitle: The shadow an object throws
cards.explanation: A cast shadow falls onto another surface and takes that surface's shape. It is darkest and sharpest near the object and grows paler and softer as it travels away.
look: The cup's shadow is crisp at its base and soft at its tip
Her shadow bends where the floor meets the wall
The shadows show exactly where the light is coming from

cards.name: Contact Shadow
cards.subtitle: The dark line where things touch
cards.explanation: Where two surfaces meet, almost no light gets in. That thin, very dark accent is what makes an object sit on a table instead of floating above it.
look: A dark sliver under the cup and saucer
Deep accents where the chair legs meet the floor
The same darkness where her crossed legs press together

images.label: Variant 1 — The control with contact shadows removed, so objects seem to…
Variant 2 — The control with strong contact shadows under cup, chair legs…

cards.name: Hard Light and Soft Light
cards.subtitle: Small source, large source
cards.explanation: A small or distant source, such as bare sun, gives hard light with sharp-edged shadows. A large or diffused source, such as a cloudy sky or a curtained window, gives soft light with gradual shadows.
look: Hard light draws crisp shadow edges and strong texture
Soft light wraps around the face and flatters it
The light's direction is identical in both pictures

images.label: Variant 1 — Hard direct sun with razor-edged shadows
Variant 2 — Very soft diffused light with barely visible shadow edges

lessons.title: Direction of Light
lessons.thesis: Move one lamp around the model and you get eight different people.
lessons.intro: Where the light comes from decides how much of the form we see and how the subject feels: open, sculpted, mysterious, heroic or frightening. In this lesson nothing changes except the position of a single light.
lessons.exercise: In a dark room, hold your phone's flashlight at arm's length and move it around your own face in a mirror: front, side, above, below, behind. Name each position using the cards.

cards.name: Front Light
cards.subtitle: Light from the camera's position
cards.explanation: Light coming from behind the viewer fills every shadow. Forms flatten and color and pattern become the main event. It is honest and friendly, and it has little depth.
look: Almost no shadows on the face
Shapes read as flat areas of color
The mood is open and plain, like a passport photo

cards.name: Three-Quarter Light
cards.subtitle: The classic portrait angle
cards.explanation: Light from about 45 degrees to the side and above shows form best: most of the face is lit and enough is shadowed to look solid. A small triangle of light on the shadowed cheek is the mark of what photographers call Rembrandt lighting.
look: About three-quarters of the face is lit
A small lit triangle sits under the eye on the shadow side
The nose casts a short shadow toward the far cheek

cards.name: Side Light
cards.subtitle: Half light, half shadow
cards.explanation: Light from 90 degrees splits the form down the middle. It reveals texture and feels dramatic or divided, which is why film uses it for characters with two sides.
look: One half of the face is lit and the other is dark
Every surface texture stands out in relief
Long shadows stretch sideways across the table

cards.name: Rim Light
cards.subtitle: Light from behind
cards.explanation: A light behind the subject traces her outline with a bright edge and leaves the front in shade. It separates a figure from a dark background and adds a touch of glamour.
look: A thin bright line runs along the hair, shoulder and arm
The face is in soft shadow
The figure pops cleanly off the background

cards.name: Top Light
cards.subtitle: Light from directly above
cards.explanation: Overhead light is the look of noon sun and ceiling fixtures. It shadows the eye sockets and under the nose and chin, and can feel harsh, lonely or interrogating.
look: The eyes sit in shadow under the brow
The top of the head and shoulders are brightest
Shadows pool directly underneath everything

cards.name: Under Light
cards.subtitle: Light from below
cards.explanation: We almost never see faces lit from beneath, so it looks unnatural at once. It is the campfire-story and horror-film light, though a glowing screen or a table candle makes it natural.
look: Shadows run upward, the reverse of normal
The chin and the underside of the nose are brightest
The face looks unfamiliar and a little eerie

cards.name: Backlit Silhouette
cards.subtitle: All light behind, none in front
cards.explanation: When the background is bright and no light reaches the front, the subject becomes a dark flat shape. Detail is traded away for outline and mood.
look: The figure is a near-black shape against a glowing window
Only the outline tells you who she is and what she is doing
The picture feels quiet and private

cards.name: Three-Point Lighting
cards.subtitle: Key, fill and rim together
cards.explanation: The standard studio setup uses three lights. The key is the main light, the fill softens its shadows from the other side, and the rim separates the subject from the background.
look: The key alone looks dramatic but harsh
Adding the fill lifts the shadows without removing them
Adding the rim outlines the hair and shoulders

images.label: Variant 1 — Key light only, from the left
Variant 2 — Fill light only, dim, from the right

lessons.title: Light Sources and Atmosphere
lessons.thesis: Light has a time, a place and a temperature. Name the source and you have named the mood.
lessons.intro: Sunset, noon, a candle and a neon sign each have their own color, hardness and direction. Viewers know these lights from life, so choosing one sets the hour and the feeling without a word. Here the café stays put while the day and the lamps change around it.
lessons.exercise: Photograph the same corner of your room at four times of day without moving anything. Lay the four photos side by side and describe the color of the shadows in each.

cards.name: Golden Hour
cards.subtitle: Low sun, shortly after sunrise or before sunset
cards.explanation: When the sun is near the horizon its light turns warm orange and arrives almost sideways. Shadows grow long and take on the cool blue of the sky, so warm and cool sit side by side.
look: Warm orange light rakes across the room
Shadows are long and bluish
Everything looks gentle and a little nostalgic

cards.name: High Noon
cards.subtitle: Sun overhead
cards.explanation: Midday sun is hard, nearly white and comes from above. Shadows are short and dark, contrast is high and colors bleach in the glare.
look: Short, hard-edged shadows directly under objects
Bright surfaces are almost washed out
The mood is exposed, hot and flat

cards.name: Overcast
cards.subtitle: The sky as one giant lamp
cards.explanation: Cloud cover spreads the sun into a huge soft source. Shadows nearly vanish, and colors show their true selves because nothing is bleached or thrown into darkness.
look: Shadows are faint and edgeless
Local colors look rich and even
The mood is calm, cool and a little subdued

cards.name: Blue Hour
cards.subtitle: Twilight, after the sun has gone
cards.explanation: For a short time after sunset the only daylight is the deep blue of the sky. Any lamp that comes on looks orange against it, giving the classic warm-against-cool evening scene.
look: The window and street are deep blue
Interior lamps glow orange by contrast
The picture feels like the day is ending

cards.name: Moonlight
cards.subtitle: Night, lit from the sky
cards.explanation: Moonlight is dim reflected sunlight, and in low light our eyes see less color and lean toward blue. Painters and filmmakers show it as cool, low-contrast and nearly colorless.
look: A narrow range of cool blue-grays
Colors are almost drained away
Shadows are soft and detail is scarce

cards.name: Candlelight
cards.subtitle: A small flame, close by
cards.explanation: A candle is a tiny, warm, nearby source. Its light fades fast with distance, so the nearest things glow and the room falls quickly into darkness.
look: The face and hands are warm orange
Brightness drops sharply a short distance from the flame
The corners of the room are nearly black

cards.name: Lamp Light
cards.subtitle: A pool of light in a dark room
cards.explanation: A shaded lamp throws a cone of warm light and leaves the rest alone. It makes a private island: everything inside the pool belongs together.
look: A bright circle on the table, falling off at its edge
The figure is half inside the pool and half outside
The darkness around it feels safe and close

cards.name: Neon and Mixed Light
cards.subtitle: Two colors of light at once
cards.explanation: City nights mix sources: pink signs, green tubes, blue screens. When two colored lights hit a form from different sides, each side takes one color and the scene turns electric.
look: One side of the face is magenta and the other cyan
Shadows from one light are filled by the other's color
Wet or glossy surfaces repeat both colors

cards.name: Dappled Light
cards.subtitle: Light through leaves
cards.explanation: Sunlight filtered through foliage or a lattice arrives as a scatter of bright patches. The pattern is lively and summery, and it partly disguises the forms it falls on.
look: Irregular spots of sun across the table and figure
The patches follow the surfaces they land on
The eye has to work a little to find the face

cards.name: Haze and Light Beams
cards.subtitle: Air you can see
cards.explanation: Dust, steam or mist in the air catches light and makes it visible as shafts. Haze also lightens and softens everything behind it, which adds depth.
look: Visible beams slant in from the window
The far wall is paler and softer than the near table
The room feels still, as if time has slowed

lessons.title: Surfaces and Materials
lessons.thesis: We recognize what a thing is made of by how it handles light.
lessons.intro: The same lamp falls on porcelain, silk, steel and skin, and each answers differently: one scatters the light, one mirrors it, one lets it through. Knowing those few behaviors lets you ask for any material by name and check whether it came out right.
lessons.exercise: Line up a paper napkin, a glazed mug, a metal spoon and a glass of water under one lamp. For each, say where the brightest spot is and how sharp its edge looks.

cards.name: Matte
cards.subtitle: Light scattered in all directions
cards.explanation: A matte surface, such as paper, plaster or unglazed clay, scatters light evenly. It has no mirror-like highlight, only a smooth shift from light to shadow.
look: No bright spots anywhere on the surface
Shading is gradual and even
The surface's own color shows clearly

cards.name: Gloss
cards.subtitle: A shine on top of a color
cards.explanation: A glossy surface, such as glazed porcelain or lacquer, is a colored body under a thin mirror. You see the object's color and, on top of it, sharp reflections of the lights and window.
look: A crisp window-shaped highlight on the cup
The cup's color is still visible around the highlight
Dark surfaces show reflections most clearly

cards.name: Metal
cards.subtitle: A surface made of reflections
cards.explanation: Polished metal has almost no color of its own to show. What you see is the room, distorted across its shape, with very bright lights right next to very dark darks.
look: Extreme contrast inside a small area
The surroundings appear bent across the form
Edges catch thin bright lines

cards.name: Glass and Liquid
cards.subtitle: Light passing through
cards.explanation: Transparent things are drawn mostly by what happens at their edges. Light bends as it passes through, so the background shifts, and bright highlights sit beside dark rims.
look: The background is visible but displaced through the glass
The rim and base carry the darkest and lightest accents
The glass throws a shadow with a bright spot inside it

cards.name: Fabric
cards.subtitle: Folds that reveal the cloth
cards.explanation: Cloth shows its weight and weave in its folds. Silk breaks into many sharp, shiny creases, while wool hangs in a few broad, soft, matte folds.
look: Silk has bright streaks along every fold
Wool has rounded folds with no shine
The drape tells you how heavy the cloth is

cards.name: Skin
cards.subtitle: Light that goes in and comes back out
cards.explanation: Skin is slightly translucent. Light enters, scatters under the surface and leaves tinted warm, which is why shadow edges on skin look reddish and thin parts such as ears glow when lit from behind.
look: The boundary between light and shadow on the face is warm
Backlit ears and fingertips glow red-orange
Without this effect, skin looks like plastic or stone

cards.name: Texture Contrast
cards.subtitle: Rough beside smooth
cards.explanation: A texture is felt most strongly next to its opposite. Placing rough against smooth, or soft against hard, makes both more vivid and gives the eye variety.
look: Rough brick behind smooth skin
Coarse knit against polished porcelain
Side light makes every rough surface stand out

lessons.title: Color Basics
lessons.thesis: Every color is three numbers: which color, how light, how strong.
lessons.intro: People say "blue" as if it were one thing. A designer hears three separate dials: hue, value and saturation. This lesson turns each dial alone, then shows the two facts that surprise beginners most: light changes the color of things, and neighbors change the color you see.
lessons.exercise: Pick any object near you and describe its color with three words, one for each dial, such as "a dark, dull orange". Brown, by the way, is exactly that.

cards.name: Hue
cards.subtitle: Which color on the wheel
cards.explanation: Hue is the color's family name: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet. Arranged in a circle they make the color wheel, the map every color scheme is drawn on.
look: Only the outfit's hue changes; lightness and strength stay equal
Each hue brings a different feeling to the same scene
Warm hues seem to advance and cool hues to recede

cards.name: Value of a Color
cards.subtitle: How light or dark it is
cards.explanation: Every color also sits somewhere between white and black. Yellow is naturally light and violet naturally dark, and two very different hues can share exactly the same value.
look: The same blue runs from near-white to near-black
The lightest version blends with the wall and the darkest with the shadows
In grayscale, the hue disappears and only this dial remains

cards.name: Saturation
cards.subtitle: How strong or gray it is
cards.explanation: Saturation, also called chroma, is the intensity of a color: from vivid, through muted, down to gray. Most of the real world is far less saturated than beginners expect.
look: The vivid version shouts and the muted one whispers
At zero saturation the picture is grayscale
The middle version looks most like real life

cards.name: Tint, Tone and Shade
cards.subtitle: Adding white, gray or black
cards.explanation: Painters name three ways to change a pure color. Add white for a tint, gray for a tone and black for a shade. A whole picture can be built from one hue this way.
look: Tints look soft and pastel
Tones look sophisticated and quiet
Shades look rich and heavy

cards.name: Temperature
cards.subtitle: Warm colors and cool colors
cards.explanation: Reds, oranges and yellows feel warm. Blues, blue-greens and violets feel cool. Temperature is relative: a color looks warm or cool mainly by comparison with its neighbors.
look: The warm version feels cozy and near
The cool version feels calm and distant
A small warm spot in a cool picture draws the eye at once

images.label: Variant 1 — Warm, toward orange and red,
Variant 2 — Cool, toward blue and teal. Lighting direction unchanged

cards.name: Local Color and Light Color
cards.subtitle: What a thing is, and what the light makes it
cards.explanation: Local color is an object's own color in neutral light. The color you actually see is local color mixed with the color of the light. A white cup is orange at sunset and blue at dusk.
look: The cup is "white" in all three pictures, and never the same color twice
Colored light tints every surface it touches
Your brain corrects for this, which is why it must be learned

cards.name: Warm Light, Cool Shadow
cards.subtitle: The rule of opposites
cards.explanation: Shadows are filled by whatever light is left over, usually of a different color from the main light. Under warm sun, shadows lean toward the blue of the sky. Under cool light, they look warm.
look: Sunlit areas are yellow-orange and their shadows are blue-violet
In the reversed version, cool light gives warm brown shadows
Shadows have color; they are never just gray

images.label: Variant 1 — Warm sunlight with distinctly cool blue shadows
Variant 2 — Cool north light with distinctly warm shadows

cards.name: Simultaneous Contrast
cards.subtitle: Colors change their neighbors
cards.explanation: The eye judges every color against what surrounds it. The same gray looks cool on orange and warm on blue, lighter on black and darker on white.
look: The cup is the identical gray in both pictures
Against orange it looks bluish, and against blue it looks warm
No color can be chosen alone, only in company

lessons.title: Color Schemes
lessons.thesis: A color scheme is a decision about which colors are invited and which are left out.
lessons.intro: Pictures that use every color equally look chaotic. Harmony comes from limits: a few hues chosen by their positions on the color wheel, in unequal amounts. Each card repaints the café with a different guest list.
lessons.exercise: Take a screenshot from a film you like and name its scheme using these cards. Then find the one small area of color that breaks the scheme. There usually is one, and it is usually the point.

cards.name: Monochromatic
cards.subtitle: One hue, many values
cards.explanation: The whole picture is built from tints, tones and shades of a single hue. It is unified by definition, and it depends entirely on value to separate one thing from another.
look: Everything belongs to one color family
Light and dark do all the describing
The mood is strong and single-minded

cards.name: Analogous
cards.subtitle: Neighbors on the wheel
cards.explanation: Three or four hues that sit side by side, such as yellow, orange and red, always agree with each other. The result is harmonious and gentle, with little tension.
look: All colors lean the same way
Transitions between areas are smooth
The mood is settled and natural, like autumn leaves

cards.name: Complementary
cards.subtitle: Opposites on the wheel
cards.explanation: Two hues from opposite sides, such as blue and orange, make each other look stronger. It is the highest-contrast pairing, and it works best when one color clearly dominates.
look: Blue fills most of the picture
Orange appears in a small, important place
Where the two touch, the edge seems to vibrate

cards.name: Split-Complementary
cards.subtitle: One color and its opposite's two neighbors
cards.explanation: Instead of the direct opposite, take the hues on either side of it: for example blue with yellow-orange and red-orange. You keep the contrast and lose some of the harshness.
look: One main hue and two related accents
Lively, and less confrontational than a straight pair
The two accents agree with each other

cards.name: Triadic
cards.subtitle: Three hues equally spaced
cards.explanation: Three colors at equal distances around the wheel, such as red, yellow and blue, give variety with balance. One should lead, or the result looks like a toy shop.
look: Three distinct color families are present
One covers most of the area
The feeling is bright, playful and energetic

cards.name: Limited Palette
cards.subtitle: Few pigments, mixed
cards.explanation: Many painters work from three or four paints. A famous example is the Zorn palette: yellow ochre, red, black and white. Because every mixture shares the same parents, the picture harmonizes itself.
look: No bright blue or green anywhere
Grays made from black stand in for the cool colors
Skin tones look especially natural

cards.name: Dominant, Secondary, Accent
cards.subtitle: Unequal amounts
cards.explanation: A common rule of thumb gives about 60 percent of the picture to one color, 30 percent to a second and 10 percent to an accent. The exact numbers do not matter. The inequality does.
look: One color clearly owns the picture
A second supports it
A third appears in a few small, deliberate spots

cards.name: Muted Field, One Accent
cards.subtitle: Saturation as a spotlight
cards.explanation: When almost everything is gray or dull, a single saturated color becomes impossible to miss. It works like a spotlight that needs no light.
look: The scene is nearly colorless
One object carries all the saturation
Your eye goes to it first and returns to it

cards.name: Color and Mood
cards.subtitle: The same room, four feelings
cards.explanation: Color choices carry emotion that viewers read without thinking. The associations vary between cultures and are not laws, but within one audience they are reliable.
look: Warm and bright feels cheerful
Cool and dark feels lonely
A greenish cast feels uneasy; soft pastels feel tender

images.label: Variant 1 — Warm, bright yellows and oranges,
Variant 4 — Soft pastel pink and lavender

lessons.title: Depth and Space
lessons.thesis: A picture is flat. Every sense of depth in it is a trick, and there are only about ten tricks.
lessons.intro: Artists make a flat surface feel deep with a small set of cues the eye already trusts from life: things overlap, shrink, converge, fade and blur. This lesson applies them one at a time, then removes them all to show that flatness is also a choice.
lessons.exercise: Stand at a window with a long view. List every cue that tells you the farthest thing is far. Most people find at least four from this lesson.

cards.name: Overlap
cards.subtitle: In front means nearer
cards.explanation: When one shape covers part of another, we read it as closer. It is the simplest and strongest depth cue, and it works even in a flat cartoon.
look: The table covers part of her legs, so it is nearer
She covers part of the window, so the window is farther
A chain of overlaps leads the eye step by step into the room

cards.name: Diminishing Size
cards.subtitle: Farther means smaller
cards.explanation: Objects we know to be the same size look smaller with distance. A row of identical things shrinking is an instant measure of space.
look: Identical tables get smaller toward the back
The far customers are a fraction of her height
The rate of shrinking tells you how deep the room is

cards.name: Horizon Line and Vanishing Point
cards.subtitle: The viewer's eye level
cards.explanation: The horizon line is the height of the viewer's eye. Level lines that run away from the viewer appear to meet at a vanishing point on it. You see the tops of things below the line and the undersides of things above it.
look: The horizon crosses the picture at her eye height
Floorboards and table edges aim toward one spot on it
You look down onto the tabletop and up under the ceiling lamps

cards.name: One-Point Perspective
cards.subtitle: Facing the room head-on
cards.explanation: When you face a wall squarely, every line going away from you meets at a single point. The effect is formal, symmetrical and tunnel-like.
look: All receding lines aim at one point behind her head
The back wall is a flat, undistorted rectangle
The room feels ordered and still

cards.name: Two-Point Perspective
cards.subtitle: Looking at a corner
cards.explanation: Turn to face a corner and the walls recede in two directions, to two vanishing points on the horizon. This is how we usually see rooms and buildings, and it feels more natural and dynamic.
look: The left wall recedes to the left and the right wall to the right
Vertical lines stay vertical
The corner of the room or table points toward the viewer

cards.name: Atmospheric Perspective
cards.subtitle: Distance through air
cards.explanation: Air is not perfectly clear. With distance, things become paler, bluer, lower in contrast and less detailed. Painters exaggerate this to push backgrounds back.
look: The near figure has the darkest darks and sharpest detail
Each layer of buildings beyond the window is paler and bluer
The farthest shapes nearly merge with the sky

cards.name: Foreground, Middle Ground, Background
cards.subtitle: Three planes
cards.explanation: Dividing a scene into three distinct layers, each with its own value, gives a clear sense of space. Stage sets and landscape paintings rely on it.
look: A dark object close to the camera frames the view
She sits in the well-lit middle
A pale, simple background closes the space

cards.name: Depth of Field
cards.subtitle: Sharp here, soft there
cards.explanation: A lens focuses at one distance. Things nearer and farther blur. Selective focus tells the viewer exactly where to look and how far away everything else is.
look: Her face is sharp
The background melts into soft discs of light
Objects very near the camera are blurred too

cards.name: Foreshortening
cards.subtitle: Forms pointing at you
cards.explanation: An arm stretched toward the viewer does not look long. It looks short, with a large hand overlapping a compressed forearm. Foreshortening is perspective applied to the body, and it creates powerful depth.
look: The offered cup and hand are very large
The forearm is hidden almost entirely behind them
The pose seems to break through the picture surface

cards.name: Flat Space
cards.subtitle: Depth switched off
cards.explanation: Many traditions and much modern design choose to stay flat: no shrinking, no converging lines, no shadows. The picture becomes a pattern on a surface.
look: Near and far objects are the same scale
The floor tilts up like a wall
Shapes sit side by side instead of one behind another

lessons.title: The Figure
lessons.thesis: You do not need to draw a body to direct one. You need the words for how it is built and how it stands.
lessons.intro: This is the one lesson where the pose changes, because the pose is the subject. Each card gives you a term that artists use to describe a figure: its proportions, its underlying forms, its line of movement, its balance and its expression. With these terms you can tell an AI exactly what is wrong with a figure and what you want instead.
lessons.exercise: Find a photo of a person standing. Draw one curved line through the whole pose from head to weight-bearing foot. Then mark the tilt of the shoulders and the tilt of the hips with two straight lines. You have just described the pose in three strokes.

cards.name: Proportion in Heads
cards.subtitle: Measuring the body with its own head
cards.explanation: Artists measure height in head-lengths. A realistic adult is about seven and a half heads tall. Fashion and heroic figures are stretched to eight or more, and cartoon characters shrink to between two and four.
look: More heads makes a figure look taller, older and more elegant
Fewer heads makes it look younger and cuter
The head itself stays the same size in all four

cards.name: Body Landmarks
cards.subtitle: Where things line up
cards.explanation: A few alignments make a figure look right. The body's midpoint is at the hips, not the waist. Elbows fall near the waist, and fingertips reach mid-thigh. On the face, the eyes sit halfway down the head.
look: The halfway line passes through the hip joint
Elbows and waist share a level, as do wrists and hips
The eyes are in the middle of the head, lower than beginners expect

cards.name: The Mannequin
cards.subtitle: The body as simple solids
cards.explanation: Under the surface, a figure is a set of basic forms: a ball for the skull, an egg for the ribcage, a box for the pelvis, cylinders for the limbs. Thinking this way makes it possible to turn a figure in space.
look: Ribcage and pelvis are two separate masses joined by a flexible waist
Each limb is two cylinders with a joint between
Light falls on the solids as it does on any sphere or cylinder

images.label: Variant 1 — A wooden artist's mannequin built from spheres, boxes and cyl…
Variant 2 — The normal figure. Same lighting

cards.name: Gesture and Line of Action
cards.subtitle: One curve through the whole pose
cards.explanation: Gesture is the overall movement of a pose, captured before any detail. The line of action is a single imaginary curve running through it. A clear C or S curve feels alive, and a straight vertical feels stiff.
look: One sweeping curve runs from head to foot
Every body part follows or balances that curve
The stiff version has the same anatomy and no life

images.label: Variant 2 — Leaning in a clear C-curve
Variant 3 — Stretching in a clear S-curve

cards.name: Weight and Balance
cards.subtitle: Where the body's weight goes
cards.explanation: A believable figure is held up by something. When standing, the head sits above the foot that carries the weight. When sitting or leaning, the weight visibly presses into the chair, table or wall.
look: A vertical line from her head lands on the supporting foot
The weight-bearing leg is straight and the other is relaxed
In the off-balance version, she looks about to fall

cards.name: Tilt and Twist
cards.subtitle: Shoulders against hips
cards.explanation: When weight shifts to one leg, the hips tilt one way and the shoulders tilt the other. This counter-tilt is called contrapposto. Twisting the chest away from the direction of the hips adds further energy.
look: The shoulder line and hip line slope in opposite directions
The spine makes a gentle S between them
The twisted version looks caught in mid-turn

images.label: Variant 3 — Contrapposto with the upper body twisted to look over her sho…

cards.name: Open and Closed Poses
cards.subtitle: Body language
cards.explanation: An open pose exposes the chest, spreads the arms and leans in. It reads as confident or welcoming. A closed pose folds the arms and legs inward and turns away, and reads as guarded, shy or cold.
look: Open: arms away from the body, chin up, leaning toward the viewer
Closed: arms crossed, shoulders raised, body angled away
The face is the same in both, and the message is opposite

images.label: Variant 2 — Closed, arms folded, turned partly away. Neutral expression i…

cards.name: Head Angle
cards.subtitle: Front, three-quarter, profile, tilt
cards.explanation: The direction and tilt of the head changes both likeness and attitude. Front view confronts, three-quarter view shows the most form, and profile is the most graphic. A tilt adds emotion.
look: Front view is symmetrical and direct
Three-quarter view shows the depth of nose and cheek
Chin down with eyes up looks intense or shy

images.label: Variant 4 — Three-quarter with chin lowered and eyes raised

cards.name: Expression
cards.subtitle: Brows, eyelids, mouth
cards.explanation: Most facial expression comes from three controls: the eyebrows, the eyelids and the corners of the mouth. Small changes to each produce every emotion, and mixed signals produce subtle ones.
look: Brows up or down, together or apart
Eyelids wide, relaxed or narrowed
Mouth corners up, level or down

cards.name: Hands
cards.subtitle: The second face
cards.explanation: After the face, viewers look at the hands. A relaxed hand, a clenched fist and a delicate fingertip grip each say something different. Hands are also where generated images fail most often.
look: Relaxed fingers curve gently and are never parallel
Tension shows in the knuckles and wrist
Count them: four fingers and a thumb on each hand

images.label: Variant 3 — Lifting it delicately by the handle with fingertips

lessons.title: Viewpoint
lessons.thesis: Before anything else, a picture answers one question: where is the viewer standing?
lessons.intro: Camera height, tilt, distance and lens decide the viewer's relationship to the subject: equal, smaller, larger, intimate or remote. Film directors call these choices shots and angles, and the same terms work for any image. Here she never moves. The camera does.
lessons.exercise: Photograph a friend, or a mug, from knee height, eye height and from a chair above. Decide which picture makes the subject look most powerful and which most vulnerable.

cards.name: Eye Level
cards.subtitle: Meeting the subject as an equal
cards.explanation: With the camera at the subject's eye height, the viewer feels like a person sitting across the table. It is neutral and natural, and it is the baseline for every other angle.
look: The horizon runs through her eyes
Nothing is distorted or exaggerated
The relationship feels equal and conversational

cards.name: Low Angle
cards.subtitle: Looking up
cards.explanation: A camera below eye level makes the subject loom. She appears taller, stronger and more important, and the ceiling or sky replaces the floor as background.
look: You see the underside of the table and her chin
The ceiling is visible and the floor is not
She looks confident, even imposing

cards.name: High Angle
cards.subtitle: Looking down
cards.explanation: A camera above eye level makes the subject smaller and the floor into the background. It can feel protective, superior or lonely, depending on what else is in the frame.
look: You see the tabletop and the top of her head
The floor fills the background
She looks smaller and more vulnerable

cards.name: Bird's-Eye View
cards.subtitle: Straight down
cards.explanation: From directly overhead, the scene becomes a map. Depth nearly disappears, people become shapes and the arrangement of objects is the whole picture.
look: The table is a perfect circle or rectangle
You see only her head, shoulders and knees
The picture reads as a flat pattern

cards.name: Worm's-Eye View
cards.subtitle: From the ground, in three-point perspective
cards.explanation: From floor level looking steeply up, vertical lines also converge, toward a third vanishing point overhead. The subject towers and the architecture soars.
look: Walls and window frames lean inward as they rise
Her shoes are huge and her head is small
The effect is monumental and a little dizzying

cards.name: Dutch Tilt
cards.subtitle: A tilted horizon
cards.explanation: Rotating the camera so the horizon slopes makes a stable scene feel wrong. Films use it for unease, confusion or sudden action.
look: The floor and table run diagonally across the frame
Verticals lean, so nothing feels secure
A calm scene becomes tense without any other change

cards.name: Shot Size
cards.subtitle: How much of the subject fills the frame
cards.explanation: Distance sets intimacy. A wide shot shows a person in a place, a medium shot shows what she is doing, a close-up shows what she feels and an extreme close-up shows a single detail.
look: Wide: the room matters as much as she does
Close-up: the face is everything
Extreme close-up: one detail becomes the whole subject

images.label: Variant 1 — Wide: whole café, full figure small
Variant 2 — Medium: waist up with the table
Variant 4 — Extreme close-up: eyes and glasses only

cards.name: Lens
cards.subtitle: Wide-angle and telephoto
cards.explanation: A wide-angle lens used up close stretches space: near things swell and the background shrinks away. A telephoto lens used from far off compresses space: the background looms large and flat behind the subject.
look: Wide: the cup and hands are large, the room is deep and its lines bend
Telephoto: the background is big, blurred and close behind her
She is the same size in both frames

images.label: Variant 1 — Wide-angle lens close to her,
Variant 2 — Long telephoto lens from across the street through the window

lessons.title: Composition
lessons.thesis: Composition is the arrangement of everything inside the rectangle. The rectangle itself is the first decision.
lessons.intro: The same figure can sit in the center or to one side, be boxed in or be given space, and be pointed at by every line in the room or by none. These arrangements have names. None of them is a rule you must obey. Each is a tool with a known effect.
lessons.exercise: Take one photo on your phone, then crop it five different ways using the cards in this lesson. Keep the crop that changes the meaning most.

cards.name: Rule of Thirds
cards.subtitle: Off-center on a three-by-three grid
cards.explanation: Divide the frame into thirds both ways. Placing the subject on one of the lines, or where two cross, usually feels more natural and dynamic than dead center.
look: Her face sits where two grid lines cross
The table edge lies along the lower third
The empty two-thirds give the picture room to breathe

cards.name: Centered Symmetry
cards.subtitle: The subject in the middle
cards.explanation: Placing the subject on the center line, with matching halves on either side, is formal, stable and commanding. It suits portraits of power, religious images and anything meant to feel deliberate.
look: Left and right halves nearly mirror each other
She faces the viewer squarely
The picture feels still, formal and a little ceremonial

cards.name: Diagonal
cards.subtitle: Energy across the frame
cards.explanation: A composition built on a slanting line feels active. The eye travels along the diagonal, and the picture seems to be in motion even when nothing moves.
look: The main shapes line up from one corner toward the opposite one
The eye slides along that line
The scene feels livelier than the level version

cards.name: Triangle
cards.subtitle: A stable three-point shape
cards.explanation: Grouping the main elements into a triangle, wide at the base and narrow at the top, gives stability and leads the eye up to the peak. Renaissance painters built portraits and group scenes this way.
look: Her head is the top point
Her elbows, or the table's edges, form the base
The shape feels solid and calm

cards.name: Leading Lines
cards.subtitle: Roads for the eye
cards.explanation: Any strong line in a picture pulls the eye along it. If the lines of the room converge on the subject, the viewer arrives there without effort.
look: Floorboards, table edges and window frames aim toward her
The eye enters at the frame's edge and travels inward
She is found at once, even though she is small

cards.name: Frame Within a Frame
cards.subtitle: A window around the subject
cards.explanation: A doorway, window or arch inside the picture can surround the subject. It focuses attention, adds depth and can make the viewer feel like an onlooker.
look: A dark doorway or window frame surrounds her
Everything outside the inner frame is quieter
The viewer seems to be looking in from another room

cards.name: Negative Space
cards.subtitle: Emptiness as a subject
cards.explanation: Leaving most of the frame empty makes a small subject more important. The emptiness becomes a feeling of its own: calm, isolation, freedom or silence.
look: She occupies a small corner of the frame
A large plain wall fills the rest
The empty area carries the mood

cards.name: Looking Room
cards.subtitle: Space in front of the gaze
cards.explanation: A figure looking to one side needs space in that direction. Give it and the picture feels comfortable. Take it away and she seems trapped or cut off.
look: With space ahead, her gaze has somewhere to go
Against the edge, she looks blocked
The only difference is where the frame was placed

images.label: Variant 1 — Placed at left with open space ahead of her gaze,
Variant 2 — Placed at right with her face close to the frame edge

cards.name: Format
cards.subtitle: The shape of the rectangle
cards.explanation: The proportions of the frame set expectations before anything is drawn. Horizontal suits places and calm, vertical suits figures and height, square is balanced and still, and a wide panorama feels cinematic.
look: Landscape gives her a room
Portrait makes her tall and important
Panorama turns the scene into a film still

cards.name: Tangents and Awkward Crops
cards.subtitle: Accidents at the edges
cards.explanation: A tangent is where two edges just touch, such as a head grazing the frame or a cup rim lining up with a chin. It flattens the space and distracts. Cropping a figure exactly at a joint looks like an amputation.
look: In the flawed version her head touches the top edge
The frame cuts her at the ankles and wrist
The corrected version overlaps clearly or leaves clear gaps

images.label: Variant 1 — Flawed: head touching the top edge, frame cutting at the ankl…
Variant 2 — Corrected: clear space above the head, cropped at mid-shin, c…

lessons.title: Principles of Design
lessons.thesis: The principles describe what the arrangement does to the viewer: where the eye lands, how it moves and whether it rests.
lessons.intro: Line, shape, value, color and space are the ingredients. The principles of design are the effects you cook with them: emphasis, balance, rhythm, unity. They are the vocabulary of critique. When a picture feels wrong, one of these is usually the reason.
lessons.exercise: Look at any picture for three seconds, then close your eyes. What did you see first, second and third? That order is the picture's hierarchy. Decide whether it is the order the maker intended.

cards.name: Focal Point
cards.subtitle: Where the eye lands first
cards.explanation: A picture needs one place that wins. The focal point is made by difference: the sharpest edge, the strongest contrast, the brightest color or the only face.
look: One area has the highest contrast and sharpest detail
Everything else is slightly quieter
Your eye returns there after wandering

cards.name: Contrast
cards.subtitle: Difference makes things visible
cards.explanation: Contrast is any strong difference: light against dark, large against small, rough against smooth, bright against dull. Without it a picture is flat. With too much everywhere, nothing stands out.
look: The low-contrast version is gentle and unclear
The high-contrast version is bold and immediate
The strongest contrast marks what matters most

images.label: Variant 1 — Low contrast in value, color and size throughout
Variant 2 — Strong contrast in value, color and size, concentrated around…

cards.name: Balance
cards.subtitle: Visual weight, left and right
cards.explanation: Every shape has visual weight. Large, dark, bright or detailed things weigh more. Symmetrical balance mirrors the two sides. Asymmetrical balance offsets a large quiet shape with a small intense one. Radial balance arranges everything around a center.
look: Symmetrical: formal and still
Asymmetrical: she is balanced by a small bright lamp far to the other side
Radial: the table, chairs and floor pattern circle around her

images.label: Variant 2 — Asymmetrical: figure at left balanced by a small bright objec…
Variant 3 — Radial: round table, circular floor pattern, figure at the ce…

cards.name: Rhythm and Repetition
cards.subtitle: A visual beat
cards.explanation: Repeating a shape, color or interval sets up a rhythm the eye follows, as the ear follows a beat. Breaking the pattern once creates an accent.
look: A row of identical lamps and chairs sets the beat
The spacing is regular
She is the one element that breaks the pattern

cards.name: Unity and Variety
cards.subtitle: Belonging together without sameness
cards.explanation: Unity means the parts look like they belong to one picture: shared colors, shapes or textures. Variety keeps it from being dull. Too much unity is boring, and too much variety is chaos.
look: The unified version repeats a few shapes and colors
The chaotic version has no two things alike
The balanced version shares a family look with a few surprises

images.label: Variant 1 — Total unity: everything in one color and shape family
Variant 2 — Total variety: every object a different color, pattern and style

cards.name: Eye Path
cards.subtitle: The route through the picture
cards.explanation: A well-arranged picture leads the eye on a journey: in, around and back to the focal point, without sliding off an edge. Lines, gazes and spots of contrast act as stepping stones.
look: The eye enters at the bright window
It moves to her face, down her arm to the cup, and along the table back up
Nothing leads out of the frame

cards.name: Scale and Proportion
cards.subtitle: How big things are relative to each other
cards.explanation: Relative size carries meaning. A small figure in a huge space feels insignificant or free. A figure that fills the frame feels important or confined.
look: Tiny figure, vast room: the place dominates
Large figure, tight room: the person dominates
Nothing but her size in the frame has changed

images.label: Variant 1 — Figure very small inside a vast, high-ceilinged café
Variant 2 — Figure filling almost the whole frame

cards.name: Detail and Rest
cards.subtitle: Busy areas and quiet areas
cards.explanation: The eye needs places to rest. Concentrating detail at the focal point and keeping other areas simple makes a picture both rich and readable. Equal detail everywhere is exhausting.
look: Fine detail on the face, hands and cup
Broad simple areas on the wall and floor
The overloaded version gives the eye nowhere to stop

images.label: Variant 1 — Detail concentrated on face, hands and cup, with simple walls…
Variant 2 — Every surface equally crowded with pattern and objects

cards.name: Gestalt Grouping
cards.subtitle: How the eye organizes what it sees
cards.explanation: The mind groups things automatically. Things close together belong together, similar things form a set, incomplete shapes get completed, and every scene is split into figure and background.
look: Proximity: objects near each other read as one group
Similarity: the red objects connect across the room
Closure: a half-hidden shape is still read as whole

images.label: Variant 1 — Proximity: table objects in two tight clusters
Variant 2 — Similarity: a few red objects scattered among neutral ones
Variant 3 — Closure: the figure seen through gaps in a slatted screen
Variant 4 — Figure and ground: flat two-color image where figure and back…

lessons.title: Mood Recipes
lessons.thesis: A mood is a combination of settings. Change several at once and the same café tells a different story.
lessons.intro: This is the capstone, and the only image lesson where more than one thing changes. Each card names a feeling and gives the recipe: light, value, color, viewpoint and composition, all taken from earlier lessons. Read the recipe, look at the picture and check that every ingredient is doing its job.
lessons.exercise: Write your own recipe for a mood not listed here, such as "bored" or "triumphant", using one term from each of five lessons. Generate it. Then change a single ingredient and see whether the mood survives.

cards.name: Cozy
cards.subtitle: Warm, close, safe
cards.explanation: Cozy is warmth in a small space. The light is low and golden, the colors are neighbors on the warm side of the wheel, and the camera sits close at eye level.
look: Lamp light: a warm pool with soft edges
Analogous oranges and browns, low contrast
Medium close-up at eye level, with soft foreground framing

cards.name: Lonely
cards.subtitle: Small, cold, far away
cards.explanation: Loneliness is distance. The figure is small, the space around her is empty, the colors are cool and drained, and the camera looks down from far off.
look: Blue hour light and a cool, muted palette
Wide shot from a high angle
Large negative space, with rows of empty chairs

cards.name: Menacing
cards.subtitle: Dark, tilted, wrong
cards.explanation: Menace comes from what cannot be seen and what looks unnatural. The picture is low key, the light comes from below or behind, and the frame is tilted.
look: Low key with most of the frame in shadow
Under light or hard rim light, with a sickly green cast
Low angle with a Dutch tilt

cards.name: Heroic
cards.subtitle: Tall, bright, centered
cards.explanation: Heroism is height and clarity. The camera looks up, the figure is centered and symmetrical, and strong light outlines her against a simpler background.
look: Low angle, centered symmetrical composition
Golden-hour key light with a bright rim
Complementary blue and orange, strong contrast

cards.name: Mysterious
cards.subtitle: Hidden, hazy, incomplete
cards.explanation: Mystery withholds information. Edges are lost, the air is thick, the face is partly hidden and the viewer watches from outside.
look: Silhouette or strong backlight in haze
Lost edges and a near-monochromatic palette
Frame within a frame, seen through a window or doorway

cards.name: Nostalgic
cards.subtitle: Soft, golden, slightly faded
cards.explanation: Nostalgia looks like memory: warm, soft and a little washed out. Light is low and golden, contrast is compressed and colors are gently muted.
look: Golden hour with dappled or hazy light
High key, narrow value range, muted warm colors
Rule-of-thirds placement, with the gaze directed out of the window

lessons.title: Studio Practice in the AI Era
lessons.thesis: When making a picture takes seconds, the work that remains is deciding what to make, judging what came out and showing the result.
lessons.intro: Art schools teach three habits alongside technique: keeping a sketchbook, giving and taking critique, and building a portfolio. All three survive the move to AI, in a changed form. This lesson has no images and no cards.
lessons.exercise: Take the last image you generated. Describe it, analyze it, interpret it and judge it in four sentences. Then write the one-line instruction for the next version.
lessons.prose:
When making a picture takes seconds, the work that remains is deciding what to make, judging what came out and showing the result.

Sketchbook: keep a repository

FolderWhat goes in it
briefs/One file per picture: the intent in one sentence, then the settings in course terms (light, palette, viewpoint, composition)
prompts/The exact prompt, model name and version, seed and settings, so the image can be made again
refs/Reference images, each with a line on what you are borrowing from it
rejects/Failed outputs, each with a line naming what went wrong
finals/The chosen images at full resolution
journal.mdDated notes on what you tried and what you learned

Five habits make it work:

  • Make one change per commit and name it in course terms, such as "key light moved from side to three-quarter". The history becomes a critique log.
  • Branch to try an alternative, and keep both.
  • Write one brief a day, however small.
  • Do master studies: take a picture you admire, write its recipe in course terms and regenerate it with your own subject. The Style Course is 105 of these.
  • Keep the rejects. They show what you learned to avoid.

Critique: what it means now

Critique was never mainly about brushwork. It is the practice of saying what a picture does, why it does it and whether that matches what was intended. AI removes the cost of execution, which leaves critique as most of the job.

It now does three things:

  1. Selection. A generator gives you a hundred competent images. Choosing one, and knowing why, is the first creative act.
  2. Diagnosis. "It feels off" cannot be typed into a prompt. Critique turns a reaction into a named cause and then into the next instruction.
  3. Meaning. A model supplies the average of what has been done before. Whether the picture says what you meant, and whether any decision in it is yours, is a question only critique asks.
ReactionDiagnosisNext instruction
"It looks flat"Front light and a narrow value rangeMove the key light to three-quarter and widen the contrast
"I don't know where to look"No focal point; equal detail everywherePut the sharpest contrast on the face and simplify the background
"She looks stiff"No line of action; shoulders and hips levelAdd contrapposto and a C-curve
"It looks like every AI image"Model defaults: centered subject, soft glossy light, orange and tealChoose the light, palette and placement yourself

Art schools teach critique in four steps, and they still apply:

  1. Describe. Say what is literally there, without opinion.
  2. Analyze. Name how it is built: light, value, color, viewpoint, composition.
  3. Interpret. Say what it communicates or feels like.
  4. Judge. Compare it with the brief. Keep, revise or discard, and name one change.

Generated images need five extra checks:

  • Physical logic. Do all shadows agree with one light source? Do receding lines converge? Do reflections match the room?
  • Figure. Check the hands, the proportions, how limbs attach and whether she is balanced.
  • Consistency. Is the character the same person in every image?
  • Defaults. Which decisions did you make, and which did the model make for you?
  • Strays. Look for garbled text, extra objects and melted details.

Critique comes from three sources:

  • You, a day later. Distance makes faults visible.
  • An AI. It is a useful first reader, and it tends to flatter. Ask for three specific weaknesses and the course term for each.
  • Other people. They are the only test of whether a picture communicates. Ask "Where did your eye go first?" and not "Do you like it?"

Portfolio: four places, four jobs

A portfolio shows judgment. Each platform shows a different part of it.

PlaceJobWhat goes there
GitHubThe process recordThe repository above, with a README per project giving the brief, key decisions and versions. It proves how you think and that results can be reproduced.
Web pageThe curated galleryYour best 10 to 20 pieces, each with a one-line intent, plus case studies showing control, variants and final. It can be published from the same repository.
YouTubeThe explanationShort narrated breakdowns: the brief, the iterations, the critique and the final, with before-and-after comparisons.
XThe daily feed and feedback loopWork in progress, single-change comparisons and one specific question per post.

Five principles apply to all four:

  • Edit hard. A portfolio is judged by its weakest piece.
  • Show decisions. Anyone can generate a good-looking image. The brief, the rejected versions and the reasons are what set you apart.
  • Build series. Twenty images exploring one idea say more than twenty unrelated ones. The Style Course is already a portfolio piece.
  • Label AI use. Name the tools and say what you directed.
  • Check rights before selling. Copyright protection for AI-generated images is uncertain and differs by country.
